chunks.title: Current role and research interests
chunks.text: Xuming Huang is a Computer Sciences undergraduate at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, with graduation expected in May 2027. His interests are systems for AI, edge inference, operating systems, and AI compilers. His current research at WukLab, UC San Diego, focuses on NPU compilers and runtimes with Professor Yiying Zhang and PhD candidate Vikranth Srivatsa.

chunks.title: Research experience
chunks.text: Xuming’s current research at WukLab, UC San Diego, focuses on efficient NPU compilers and inference runtimes. His other research includes LinuxGuard at ADSL, UW–Madison, using LLMs and compiler feedback to build Linux-kernel bug detectors; an honors project with Michael Swift measuring how filesystem activity affects AI inference; and CASH at USST, studying workload-aware CPU/GPU scheduling. He also coauthored studies of self-supervised laryngoscopic image classification and near-infrared tunable filters.

chunks.title: Vikranth Srivatsa collaboration
chunks.text: Xuming works with Vikranth Srivatsa, a PhD candidate at WukLab, UC San Diego, on NPU compilers and runtimes. Professor Yiying Zhang advises the research.

chunks.title: Research advisors
chunks.text: Xuming’s current advisor at WukLab, UC San Diego, is Professor Yiying Zhang. His LinuxGuard advisors at ADSL, UW–Madison, were Professor Remzi Arpaci-Dusseau and Dr. Vinay Banakar. Professor Michael Swift advised his honors operating-systems project. Professor Xing Hu advised his USST scheduling research.

chunks.title: Edge AI Systems Optimization
chunks.text: Xuming is currently an undergraduate researcher at WukLab, UC San Diego, advised by Professor Yiying Zhang, since January 2026. He works with Vikranth Srivatsa, a PhD candidate at WukLab. He developed a JIT NPU runtime that overlaps CPU graph compilation with NPU inference and grows the KV cache with context: 91.98% less foreground compilation time and 33.05% lower average KV memory, while preserving model quality and decoding. Cached sorted compiler dependency vectors to reduce CPU sorting time by 94.2%, and built CPU/GPU/NPU benchmarks to guide device placement.
aliases: What research are you doing at WukLab?

chunks.title: Operating Systems for AI Inference
chunks.text: Xuming completed an honors course research project with Professor Michael Swift at UW–Madison from January to May 2026. He measured how background filesystem reads interfere with a fixed LLM inference workload: median latency increased 17.1%. Windows PerfMon showed stable working sets and page-fault counts plateauing near 29.5K, supporting shared-resource contention as the explanation rather than working-set thrashing.

chunks.title: LinuxGuard: AI for System Security
chunks.text: Xuming worked on LinuxGuard at The ADvanced Systems Laboratory (ADSL), UW–Madison, from January to November 2025, advised by Professor Remzi Arpaci-Dusseau and Dr. Vinay Banakar. Remzi was his research advisor. He built an LLM-driven pipeline over 50K+ Linux kernel commits to generate Clang-Tidy analyzers. Clustering and compiler-feedback repair produced 4× more valid checkers at 73% precision. A full-kernel validation harness uncovered 43 long-latent bugs with an average age of 4.7 years.
aliases: What research did you do with Professor Remzi Arpaci-Dusseau?

chunks.title: ML-Guided Scheduling for Heterogeneous Compute Systems
chunks.text: Xuming contributed as a coauthor and undergraduate researcher advised by Professor Xing Hu at USST, January 2024–September 2026. He contributed to experimental validation and performance analysis of CASH, which predicts workload–hardware affinity for CPU/GPU placement. In 5,000-task simulations using MIT Supercloud traces, the scheduler achieved 97.1% resource-matching accuracy, 46.5% lower response time, and 36.8% lower modeled energy than Meta-RHDC.

chunks.title: Self-Supervised Learning for Laryngoscopic Image Classification
chunks.text: Xuming is a coauthor of the BEIT-style laryngoscopic image classification paper published at ICFTIC in 2025. He coauthored a study using BEIT-style masked image pretraining to learn from unlabeled laryngoscopic images before fine-tuning for disease classification. The paper reports 93.33% accuracy on a three-class task using a ViT-Tiny backbone with 5.06 million parameters.

chunks.title: Near-Infrared Tunable Filters
chunks.text: Xuming is a coauthor of the near-infrared tunable filter paper published in Micro & Nano Letters in 2025. He coauthored a study of a voltage-tunable near-infrared filter combining polymer-dispersed liquid crystals with a Fabry–Perot cavity. The paper reports a tuning range of 913–969 nm and 99% transmittance at 927 nm, with a 24 nm full width at half maximum.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes
chunks.text: My current work at WukLab, advised by Professor Yiying Zhang , asks how to make local AI inference practical on NPUs. An accelerator can execute a model efficiently once the program is ready, but getting it ready can require substantial CPU compilation and memory allocation. Those costs matter to an interactive application.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes
chunks.text: I have been working on two connected projects: reducing repeated work inside the NPU compiler, and building a runtime that prepares larger programs while inference is already running. Together, they address both how much compilation costs and when the application has to wait for it.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes
chunks.text: In this post: Compiler optimization | Compile ahead | Grow memory with context | Next questions

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Inside an NPU
chunks.text: NPUs organize many processing elements (PEs) to perform repeated multiply-and-accumulate operations. In the weight-stationary arrangement below, weights are preloaded from SRAM into the array. Activations move through the processing elements, while partial sums accumulate toward the output. Keeping data close to the arithmetic reduces the need to repeatedly fetch it from farther away.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Inside an NPU
chunks.text: A weight-stationary processing-element array. This is a conceptual architecture illustration, not a diagram of a specific Intel NPU implementation.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Inside an NPU
chunks.text: The compiler maps a model's operations and tensor shapes onto this execution structure. The runtime then manages when compiled programs run and where their inputs, outputs, and persistent state live. That division explains why compiler preparation and memory management matter alongside the arithmetic itself.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Why the runtime matters
chunks.text: Autoregressive inference changes as it runs: every generated token extends the context and adds key and value state to the KV cache. In the static-shape NPU path studied here, compiled programs require concrete tensor dimensions. The runtime must decide which shapes to compile, how much memory to reserve, and when to move to a larger program.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Why the runtime matters
chunks.text: A straightforward design prepares a large context window before the first token. This makes execution simple, but a short request pays for capacity it may never use. Preparing several sizes in advance improves shape selection while retaining the cost of compiling them all before serving the request. These are systems decisions around the model, and they can dominate the experience even when the NPU executes individual operators quickly.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Project 1: remove repeated compiler work
chunks.text: Problem. The compiler repeatedly needs dependency and consumer lists in a deterministic order. Sorting those lists on every lookup repeats CPU work when the underlying dependency graph has not changed. A hot helper can accumulate significant work even when each individual sort is small.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Project 1: remove repeated compiler work
chunks.text: Idea. Cache the sorted dependency and consumer vectors. On an unchanged graph, a later lookup can reuse the ordered result. When a mutation changes the relevant relationships, invalidate the affected cache so the next lookup rebuilds it.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Project 1: remove repeated compiler work
chunks.text: The difficult part is maintaining the contract around graph updates. A stale list can silently change scheduling behavior. The optimization therefore has to account for mutation paths and preserve the ordering expected by callers; simply storing the first answer is not sufficient.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Project 1: remove repeated compiler work
chunks.text: This project reduces the amount of compilation work. The runtime project addresses a different question: how much of the remaining work must sit on the application's critical path?

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Project 2: compile ahead, not up front
chunks.text: Problem. Waiting until a request reaches the end of its compiled context window causes a pause while the next program is prepared. Compiling every future window at startup avoids that boundary pause, but delays the first useful inference and may prepare programs that the request never reaches.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Project 2: compile ahead, not up front
chunks.text: Idea. Start with a small program and compile a larger one on the CPU while the NPU continues inference. Keep preparation ahead of context growth. Before switching, ensure that the next program is ready and that the live KV state can be carried forward correctly.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Project 2: compile ahead, not up front
chunks.text: In the one-ahead design, the current program executes while the next size is being prepared. It bounds speculative work compared with compiling every size immediately. It also gives the compiler more time than a design that starts compilation only at the boundary.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Project 2: compile ahead, not up front
chunks.text: CPU compilation overlaps NPU inference. Original concept drawing by Vikranth Srivatsa .

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Project 2: compile ahead, not up front
chunks.text: The overlap is useful only if preparation finishes before it is needed. A fast decoder, a large compilation step, or contention for shared resources can consume that margin. Foreground waiting and total CPU work must therefore be measured separately: moving work into the background does not make it free.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Let KV memory grow with the context
chunks.text: Progressive compilation alone does not make memory use proportional to the request. A runtime can select a small graph while still reserving the largest KV buffer. To address that, the runtime starts with capacity suited to the current context and grows it when needed.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Let KV memory grow with the context
chunks.text: At a growth boundary, it allocates the next capacity, copies the live KV state, binds the new program, and continues decoding. The sequence length, positions, and cached state must remain consistent across the switch. The copy itself also has a cost, and the old and new allocations may temporarily coexist.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Let KV memory grow with the context
chunks.text: Use the smallest suitable capacity and carry the live state forward. Original concept drawing by Vikranth Srivatsa .

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — What I measure
chunks.text: I separate startup compilation, background compilation, waiting at a boundary, state transfer, and steady-state decoding. I also track memory as context grows and check output correctness across program switches. This makes it possible to tell whether an improvement removes work, overlaps it, or merely shifts it elsewhere.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — What I measure
chunks.text: The two projects complement each other. Caching compiler results can shorten preparation, while progressive compilation gives the CPU a window in which to perform that preparation. Copy-and-grow addresses the allocation side. Their percentages measure different quantities and cannot be added into one speedup.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Broader questions for NPU systems
chunks.text: I am also measuring CPU, GPU, and NPU placement preferences at the operator and inference-stage levels. The best device depends on the operation, shape, and cost of crossing device boundaries. An operator-level win is useful evidence, but it does not by itself establish an end-to-end scheduling improvement.

chunks.title: Making NPU Inference Practical: Compiler Optimization and JIT Runtimes — Broader questions for NPU systems
chunks.text: The next questions are how to adapt compilation lead time to the request, reduce state-transfer costs, and account for shared-resource contention. These are ongoing directions. The broader goal is to make compilation, memory, and device placement respond to the workload as it unfolds.

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — My Journey with LinuxGuard
chunks.text: Over the past six months (since May 2025), I have been working with Vinay Banakar on the LinuxGuard project. It was a journey that took me deep into the intersection of Large Language Models and Systems security, taught me the rigors of academic research, and ultimately ended with a valuable lesson on the fast-paced nature of computer science.

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — The Spark
chunks.text: LinuxGuard started from a simple observation about the Linux kernel: today, the kernel suffers from many performance anti‑patterns and logical bugs. There are entire releases that focus almost entirely on bug fixes—missing defaults in switch cases, failure to return 0 on success, and so on.

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — The Spark
chunks.text: Our core idea was: Can an LLM learn the kernel‑specific "DOs and DON’Ts" from commit history, and then help us create a set of checkers to automatically detect them?

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — The Spark
chunks.text: Because the kernel uses its own C coding style that does not fully conform to typical C anti‑pattern definitions, standard tools often miss these nuances. We wanted to build a system that could "read" a fix and "write" a tool to prevent that bug forever.

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — Building the Pipeline
chunks.text: To make this concrete, I began by diving into LLVM and compilers. I discovered we could generate checkers as plug‑ins, compiled directly into the Linux module of clang‑tidy . This became our vehicle for turning LinuxGuard into a practical tool.

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — Building the Pipeline
chunks.text: However, it wasn't as simple as asking ChatGPT to "write a checker."

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — Building the Pipeline
chunks.text: Chain-of-Thought Prompting: I realized that a single API call couldn't reliably synthesize correct checkers. I built a pipeline that first analyzes the anti‑pattern and then generates the checker, using a one‑shot example for guidance.

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — Building the Pipeline
chunks.text: Self-Correction: Generated checkers often failed to compile. We introduced a self‑check, repair, and reset mechanism to handle this automatically.

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — Building the Pipeline
chunks.text: Agentic Validation: The trickiest part was precision. To fight false positives, we experimented with calling a second agent—an advanced, web‑based LLM—to act as a "reviewer" for the issues found by our checkers.

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — The "KNighter" Discovery
chunks.text: Research is a race. Ultimately and unfortunately, in early November we discovered a paper published at SOSP called KNighter . They proposed almost exactly the same idea and had already implemented it effectively.

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — The "KNighter" Discovery
chunks.text: I tried to identify critical improvements or new angles we could bring to build on KNighter, but given the uncertainty and the strength of their implementation, we eventually chose to stop the project. It was frustrating to stop a project we had invested so much time in, but it is part of the game.

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — Lessons Learned
chunks.text: Despite the outcome, I learned a great deal from Vinay throughout this process. We met weekly without interruption, using a shared doc and slide deck to stay aligned.

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — Lessons Learned
chunks.text: Vinay shared one piece of advice that really shaped how I view research:

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — Lessons Learned
chunks.text: This helped me understand the difference between industry and academia. We scaled up from highly specific pattern‑matching to general checkers, and discovered that simply merging commits doesn't work—you need clustering and selection.

chunks.title: My Journey with LinuxGuard — Lessons Learned
chunks.text: Throughout all of this, Vinay has been both a mentor and a friend, always finding time for our meetings voluntarily, even when his schedule was already full. LinuxGuard may be over, but the skills I gained—in LLMs, compilers, and research methodology—are just beginning to pay off.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms
chunks.text: Spending my summer at Stanford was an incredible academic journey. I took two challenging courses that fundamentally changed how I think about computer science: CS107 Computer Organization & Systems and CS161 Design and Analysis of Algorithms . Both courses pushed me to my limits and helped me grow as a computer scientist.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms
chunks.text: Quick Links: Courses: CS107 | CS161 People: Adam Keppler | Ola Adekola | Ben Yan | Alex Keller | Matthew Sotoudeh

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — CS107: Deep Dive into Systems
chunks.text: CS107 is my favorite course this summer, and I'm proud to say I earned an A+ (99/100) . The homework was exceptionally well designed and perfectly solidified the knowledge we learned in lectures—it was my favorite part, super interesting, and I learned tremendously from each assignment.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Assignment 7: Heap Allocator
chunks.text: This was my absolute favorite assignment. Not only did I complete all the required functions, but I also finished all the challenge functions that weren't required. I wanted to see how far I could push myself, and I made it! I created a new structure that adds a footer at the end of free blocks to find the previous block, implementing a bidirectional free list that significantly improved allocation efficiency.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Assignment 7: Heap Allocator
chunks.text: → View my interactive Heap Allocator Visualization An educational visualization demonstrating the concepts from this assignment

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Assignment 6: Banking on Security
chunks.text: The Security Bomb assignment was one of the most intriguing challenges I've ever encountered. I successfully found vulnerabilities in the virtual bank and "stole the money"—all in a controlled, educational environment, of course! This assignment inspired me to explore real-life vulnerabilities.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Assignment 6: Banking on Security
chunks.text: Security Contribution to Stanford: Going beyond the assignment, I discovered critical vulnerabilities in Stanford's AFS (Andrew File System). Following responsible disclosure practices learned in the course, I:

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Assignment 6: Banking on Security
chunks.text: Submitted a detailed report following Stanford's disclosure protocols

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Assignment 6: Banking on Security
chunks.text: Huge thanks to Adam Keppler for helping me connect with the corresponding engineer, and to Alex Keller from the engineering team—we had a very productive conversation about system security and implementing the solutions I proposed.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Adam Keppler - The Inspiring Instructor
chunks.text: Adam 's teaching is simply amazing. He showed up to every single lecture with no exceptions, even though we had two instructors. His dedication was inspiring. We had wonderful conversations about computer systems concepts, my discovery of vulnerabilities, life, and everything in between.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Adam Keppler - The Inspiring Instructor
chunks.text: I had never used GDB before this course, and I excitedly told him that I found a way to bypass the "bank protection alert" in our security assignment. He appreciated that I was a quick learner and encouraged me to explore further.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Adam Keppler - The Inspiring Instructor
chunks.text: "I always asked tons of questions in lectures (that's pretty much why I sat in the first row!). Even when some questions were basic, Adam patiently answered my confusion and followed my thanks with a big smile and 'Absolutely!' His positive responses always inspired and encouraged students to think deeply."

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Adam Keppler - The Inspiring Instructor
chunks.text: I genuinely believe Adam's teaching style and encouragement were key factors in my success in this course.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Ola Adekola - Making Complex Topics Accessible
chunks.text: Big thanks to Ola! Ola's humorous tone and teaching style made dense or potentially boring content feel interesting and relaxing. The analogies and live demos helped me connect the dots between lecture material and assignments in ways I hadn't expected.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Ola Adekola - Making Complex Topics Accessible
chunks.text: After class, Ola was always friendly and open to questions, offering clear explanations of complex concepts that really helped solidify my understanding. Whether it was pointer arithmetic or assembly language intricacies, Ola had a way of making everything click.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Ben Yan - The Best TA I've Ever Met
chunks.text: Ben Yan (he/they) is, without a doubt, the best TA I have ever met. Their slides weren't just informative—they were engaging and sometimes even entertaining. Ben's teaching was super fluent, like that of a seasoned lecturer, and the meticulous, rigorous comments on our homework were incredibly helpful.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Ben Yan - The Best TA I've Ever Met
chunks.text: Ben's discussion section was the highlight of my week. They had this remarkable ability to break down complex topics into digestible pieces while maintaining technical rigor. Their feedback on assignments went above and beyond, often including additional resources and suggestions for further exploration. Ben's dedication to student success and their passion for systems programming made every session invaluable.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Alex Keller - Security Expert and Mentor
chunks.text: A huge thanks to Alex Keller , Stanford's Senior Systems Security Engineer, who took time from his busy schedule to discuss the AFS vulnerabilities I discovered. Our productive conversation covered not just the technical aspects of the security issues, but also broader topics about systems security and career paths in the field.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Alex Keller - Security Expert and Mentor
chunks.text: What struck me most was Alex's philosophy: "If you do good work at Stanford, you will be rewarded with opportunities to do more good work." This perspective helped me understand that contributing to Stanford's security through responsible disclosure was valuable experience in itself—and motivation to continue learning and contributing wherever possible.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Alex Keller - Security Expert and Mentor
chunks.text: Alex brings unique expertise to Stanford, having coached Stanford Applied Cyber for 10 years. During our meeting, he showed me the team's training facilities and shared insights about competitive cybersecurity. His dedication recently paid off with Applied Cyber winning 1st place in both the ICS (Industrial Control Systems) and Goldbug CTFs in Las Vegas—an impressive achievement for the team.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Alex Keller - Security Expert and Mentor
chunks.text: Our discussion ranged from technical details of AFS architecture to life experiences and personal journeys. Alex's willingness to mentor students and dedication to helping students with passion to chase their dream made our conversation particularly valuable. It's a shame that we didn't take a pic together but I believe we will see soon!

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Key Takeaways
chunks.text: CS 107 wasn't just about learning C programming or understanding computer architecture—it was about developing a systems mindset. Through this course, I:

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Key Takeaways
chunks.text: Gained practical experience with debugging tools like GDB and Valgrind

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Key Takeaways
chunks.text: Made real-world security contributions to Stanford's infrastructure

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Key Takeaways
chunks.text: Built lasting connections with amazing instructors and engineering team

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — CS161: The Art of Algorithm Analysis
chunks.text: CS161 Design and Analysis of Algorithms was equally transformative, earning me an A (93/100) . Before this course, I was lost in the maze of algorithmic complexity. How do you compare quicksort to mergesort? Why does one hash table outperform another? The sheer variety of algorithms and performance metrics seemed overwhelming.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — CS161: The Art of Algorithm Analysis
chunks.text: CS161 taught me the fundamental philosophy that changed everything: evaluate algorithms analytically, not just empirically. Instead of just running code and timing it, we learned to ask deeper questions:

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — CS161: The Art of Algorithm Analysis
chunks.text: Input Analysis: What happens in the best, worst, and average cases?

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — CS161: The Art of Algorithm Analysis
chunks.text: Algorithm Decisions: How do pivot choices in quicksort or hash functions affect performance?

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — CS161: The Art of Algorithm Analysis
chunks.text: Amortized Analysis: What's the cost over a sequence of operations, not just one?

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — CS161: The Art of Algorithm Analysis
chunks.text: This systematic approach transformed abstract concepts into concrete tools. Whether analyzing AVL tree rotations, understanding why hash tables achieve O(1) average time, or proving lower bounds for comparison sorting, the course provided a rigorous framework for thinking about efficiency.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Matthew Sotoudeh - The Algorithm Master
chunks.text: Huge thanks to Matthew Sotoudeh ! I'm also hugely impressed by his written materials ( CS161 Notes ). Matthew considered everything comprehensively—the thinking behind lectures (I mean the pace and step-by-step depth) and even the snacks for asking questions were awesome!

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Matthew Sotoudeh - The Algorithm Master
chunks.text: He always repeats and interprets the questions asked by other students, which is so helpful because I sometimes couldn't hear or didn't understand what they said. This thoughtful approach made complex algorithm analysis accessible to everyone.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Projects Inspired by CS161
chunks.text: The algorithm concepts from CS161 directly inspired several of my visualization projects:

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Projects Inspired by CS161
chunks.text: Sorting Algorithm Visualizer - Interactive visualization of quicksort, mergesort, heapsort showing O(n log n) complexity

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Projects Inspired by CS161
chunks.text: Graph Algorithms Playground - BFS, DFS, Dijkstra's shortest path, and A* pathfinding with complexity analysis

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Projects Inspired by CS161
chunks.text: Hash Function & Collision Analysis - Demonstrating hash tables, collision resolution, and amortized O(1) operations

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Looking Forward
chunks.text: My summer at Stanford fundamentally changed how I think about computer science. CS107 gave me deep systems knowledge while CS161 provided the analytical tools to evaluate and design efficient algorithms. The combination of theoretical knowledge and hands-on implementation has given me confidence to tackle complex problems.

chunks.title: Stanford Summer: Where Systems Meet Algorithms — Looking Forward
chunks.text: To anyone considering Stanford's summer session: these courses are challenging but incredibly rewarding. With passionate instructors and a supportive community, you're not just learning material—you're developing a new way of thinking about computation.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI
chunks.text: Last week, I had the incredible opportunity to intern at CoolAI , where I was tasked with developing AI products.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI
chunks.text: My main responsibilities included preparing a demo and materials for an interview with China Business Network (CBN) and representing CoolAI at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC).

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI
chunks.text: During the conference, I introduced our company's core business and provided detailed explanations of our products.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI — CBN Interview
chunks.text: In preparing for the interview with CBN , I meticulously worked on creating a comprehensive demo showcasing our latest AI innovations.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI — CBN Interview
chunks.text: This task required not only technical proficiency but also the ability to communicate complex ideas clearly and engagingly. The process was both challenging and rewarding, as it allowed me to refine my workflow skills and deepen my understanding of our AI solutions.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI — WAIC
chunks.text: At WAIC, I took on the role of a promoter, presenting CoolAI's cutting-edge technologies to a diverse audience. This experience was truly eye-opening.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI — WAIC
chunks.text: I was struck by the level of interest and enthusiasm from attendees, which included professionals from hundreds of internet corporations and numerous AI enthusiasts. Engaging with such a vibrant community reinforced my passion for AI and highlighted the immense potential and rapid growth of the field.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI — WAIC
chunks.text: The scale of the conference and the breadth of innovations on display were overwhelming. Witnessing firsthand the thriving nature of the AI industry and its promising future was inspiring.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI — WAIC
chunks.text: The conference underscored the rapid advancements being made and the potential for AI to transform various sectors. This realization has only solidified my ambition and dedication to pursue a career in AI.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI — Reflection
chunks.text: Reflecting on my week-long internship, I realized there is a significant difference between academic learning and professional work.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI — Reflection
chunks.text: While my studies have provided a solid theoretical foundation, the hands-on experience of working on a real-world project brought a new sense of accomplishment. The project was demanding and exhausting, yet incredibly fulfilling.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI — Reflection
chunks.text: It offered a taste of the challenges and rewards that come with working in the tech industry.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI — Conclusion
chunks.text: It not only enhanced my technical skills but also provided invaluable insights into the dynamic world of AI. The experience has strengthened my resolve to continue my journey in this exciting field, and I am more motivated than ever to contribute to its development.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI — Conclusion
chunks.text: I look forward to leveraging the knowledge and skills gained during this internship as I advance in my career.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI — Conclusion
chunks.text: This internship was a pivotal moment in my academic and professional journey, providing a bridge between the theoretical knowledge gained in the classroom and the practical skills required in the workforce.

chunks.title: Diving into AI: My Transformative First Week at CoolAI — Conclusion
chunks.text: I am grateful for the opportunity and excited about the future possibilities in the field of AI！
